title: regional-fabric-decision-log-active-mesh-fallback
body:
Purpose:
Capture trade-offs and a preferred topology for Redwood’s control plane across regions. Focus areas: routing policy behavior, leader election approaches, and disaster recovery modes for control-plane state and metadata (model versions, rollouts, routing rules).

Context / constraints:
- Goal: make inference routing predictable (latency SLOs), cost-aware, and resilient across regions without a large ops burden.
- Control plane holds critical metadata: route rules, rollout config, model pins, quota maps, and billing events. Some of these are latency-sensitive reads (route lookups), some are strongly-consistent writes (billing, legal audit logs).
- We operate in 3+ cloud regions per customer (NA, EU, APAC). We need a pattern that scales to more regions later.
- Preference for incremental rollout: start with simpler active-passive for some stores, iterate to active-active where safe.

Scenarios we must support:
1) regional outage (single-region cut) — keep majority of traffic online with minimal config drift
2) partition (region network isolation) — avoid split-brain writes for authoritative records
3) rapid spike in one region — routing should divert to healthy regions without manual ops
4) cross-region rollout (canary in a region then global) — control plane must support atomic-ish rollouts or safe progressive rollout

Topology options considered (high level):
A) Fully active-active control plane (global consensus-backed metadata store)
   - single logical cluster spans regions via strongly-consistent store (e.g., Spanner/CockroachDB with multi-region configs or global etcd mesh)
   - Pros: simpler operational model (one source of truth), immediate visibility of rollouts everywhere
   - Cons: higher write latency (cross-region median RTT), more costly, harder offline operation per-region, complex failover when partitions occur

B) Active-passive per-customer (region primary with async replicas)
   - each customer pins a primary region for writes; replicas in other regions are read-only until failover
   - Pros: very low write latency for primary region, predictable failure mode, simpler causal guarantees
   - Cons: manual or semi-automated failover for region loss, stale reads if relying on rep lag, possible poor UX for multi-region customers

C) Hybrid active-active with per-object single-writer leases (preferred draft)
   - most metadata reads are served locally from eventually-consistent replicas; writes are gated by short region-scoped leases/leases-per-namespace. A lightweight global coordination service grants write leases for critical objects.
   - Use eventual replication for route rules and rollout flags, but require lease to promote a region to accept writes for a given namespace (customer or resource table).
   - Pros: low read latency, controlled write ownership to avoid split-brain, fast local reads during partitions, more flexible failover
   - Cons: added complexity in lease management, still requires robust reconciliation loops to handle conflicts

Leader election primitives evaluated:
- Cloud-provided leader election (e.g., GCP/ALB health checks + regional primary via LB failover): simple but opaque and limited for cross-region coordination.
- Lease-based using a global KV with short TTL (e.g., Dynamo-style conditional writes): low-latency and can be implemented on top of many stores, but needs careful clock/clock-skew handling.
- Raft-based consensus (etcd/consul) per-global-cluster: strong safety, but multi-region Raft is very sensitive to latency and failure-scenarios unless using read-local, write-majority and provisioning cross-region votes.
- Quorum leases (W-lease): combine majority consensus for lease grant with local short leases to bound leader time.

Recommended leader model for hybrid topology:
- Use per-customer (or per-namespace) short-duration write leases backed by a global coordinator service. Coordinator persists lease metadata to a multi-region, moderately consistent store (CockroachDB with follower reads enabled or Spanner).
- Lease semantics: 10s-30s lease TTL with renewals by owner region. If lease is lost/unrenewed, another region can attempt to acquire. Lease acquisition requires a conditional transaction (compare-and-set) in the global store.
- For extra safety on critical writes (billing, compliance events), require two-phase commit style handoff: primary writes locally and also submit an append-only event to the global audit store which is multi-region strongly-consistent.

Routing policy implications:
- Routing decisions are read-heavy and latency-sensitive. Keep routing cache local in each region with very small TTLs for dynamism (1–5s for many policy entries).
- Policy precedence: health > latency SLO > capacity > cost preference > geo constraints. Implement policy evaluation in the edge/routing tier with ability to consult local policy cache and fallback to control-plane on cache miss.
- For global outages, routing should default to: prefer healthy local region, then nearest healthy region by RTT, then capacity-tier fallback (dedicated -> hosted), then last-resort degrade (reject or queued).

DR modes and failover sequences (concrete flows):
- Regional outage (routes and metadata):
  1) Edge detects region unreachability (health checks + control-plane lease expiry for region-owned writes).
  2) Local routers flush cached routes that reference the failed region. Fall back to latency/geo-based alternatives.
  3) Coordinator: if primary lease not renewed after TTL+grace, other regions can attempt lease acquisition.
  4) Reconcile: new owner replays any pending writes from write-ahead logs or from client replays.

- Split-brain prevention:
  - Never allow two concurrent leases for same (customer, resource) pair. Use CAS on global store to enforce single-writer.
  - On network partition, allow reads locally but queue writes until lease is established. Writes should either fail-fast or be accepted only if local lease is active.

Data plane implications (model metadata, rollouts, cache):
- Model manifests and versions: treat as eventually-consistent configuration with version stamps. When a region becomes writer, it increments manifest version and writes a signed manifest entry to the global log. Consumers treat higher version as authoritative.
- KV cache (prefix/KV cache): keep local caches warm; reconcile on reconnect using changefeed or checkpointed sequence numbers.
- Audit & billing: append-only authoritative store must be strongly consistent and replicated (multi-region Spanner or cloud DB with strong consistency). Don’t try to make billing writes fast by relaxing durability.

Operational playbooks / runbooks (high level):
- Failover test cadence: quarterly simulated region outage runbooks. Validate lease acquisition, cache reconciliation, and tail-latency during failover. Capture SLO burn metrics.
- Emergency failover: provide a controlled UI in console to force-promote a region’s lease for a customer (requires 2-person approval). Log action to audit store.
- Observability: surface lease holders per-namespace, lease TTLs, last-renew times, and reconciliation backlog size in Console.

Decision record (recommended):
- Start with hybrid approach (C) for the control plane for 2026 Q1 pilot on lower-risk namespaces (routing, rollouts).
- Use short-duration global leases with conditional CAS on CockroachDB in multi-region config.
- Maintain a separate strongly-consistent append-only store for audit/billing (Spanner or equivalent) that is only written by the current lease-holder.
- Keep routing caches local with small TTLs and implement graceful degrade priorities in the routing tier.

Open questions / TODOs:
- TTL sizing: 10–30s is starter guidance. Need experiments: measure time-to-failover and stale-read impact under simulated partitions. (JIRA: PLAT-2401)
- Implementation choice for global coordinator: a small Go service using conditional CDC from Cockroach vs leveraging an existing raft cluster — spike both. (GH PRs noted above)
- UX: how much manual override do we expose in Console? Need legal/ops input for emergency promotion gating.
- Cost model: estimate cross-region traffic for lease refresh and replication and compare to full active-active charge. (Finance ask queued)

Immediate next steps:
- Spike: implement lease-acquire/renew using Cockroach multi-region setup and a tiny coordinator. Test under packet loss simulator. Owner: Asha. Due: 2025-12-20.
- Runbook draft for emergency promotion and audit log. Owner: Lina. Due: 2025-12-10.
- Add metrics hooks to routing tier to surface TTL hits, fallback frequency, and reconciliation backlogs. Owner: Tom. Due: 2025-12-15.

Notes / informal thoughts:
- Prefer patterns that let us operate per-customer: many large customers will want a single-region primary but still expect global failover. Namespace-scoped leases map well to that requirement.
- We should avoid global synchronous writes for high-volume control-plane events (e.g., frequent rollout toggles). Instead, leverage a global event-log for eventual reconcilers and local immediate writes for serving decisions.

References:
- Short write lease paper notes (link in Confluence)
- Existing multiregion control plane experiments: see GH/PLAT spikes

Unresolved: how to handle long network partitions where two regions both think they can serve (rare but must have a clear reconciliation path). Prefer deterministic tombstone/resolution (higher version or signed decision from audit store) rather than human-only conflict resolution.

End of draft.
